# Water Reservoir Level Control Laboratory

This case study documents a functional water-level control platform developed for vocational PLC and automation education.

The system combines industrial instrumentation, electronic signal conditioning, PLC programming, electromechanical actuation, and a physical water process. It was designed as a modular and replicable laboratory rather than as a single demonstration prototype.

## Authentic Engineering Problem

The original design used an industrial **4–20 mA water-level sensor**, while the available PLC accepted voltage-based analog inputs. Rather than replacing either component, the laboratory uses an intermediate signal-conditioning stage to preserve the industrial sensor while making its signal compatible with the available control hardware.

The small physical reservoir introduced a second constraint: the usable sensor output initially occupied only approximately **1 V to 1.9 V**, wasting much of the PLC analog-input range. The conditioning circuit therefore expands the effective measurement span to approximately **1–10 V**, improving usable resolution while maintaining proportionality to water level.

Electrical noise and process dynamics also produced unstable readings and excessive pump cycling. The implemented solution combines **hardware filtering** with **software hysteresis and temporal logic**.

## Functional System Path

**Water Level → 4–20 mA Sensor → Signal Conditioning → PLC Analog Input → Scaling / Decision Logic → Relay Output → DC Pump → Reservoir**

This complete path allows students to connect instrumentation theory to an observable physical process.

## Educational Role

The project integrates concepts from electronics, electromechanics, and programmable control. Students encounter analog signals only after developing a foundation in PLC safety, I/O wiring, sourcing/sinking, sequential control, timers, counters, and digital sensors.

Laboratory 11 explicitly bridges the transition from digital to analog control and prepares students for the project by organizing the signal path as:

**Sensor → PLC Input → Raw Value → Converted Value → Ladder Decision → Output Action**
